description: The hand-verified expected result for the negative Checkov fixture whose one defective failed check carries an anchor field that cannot be expressed as a path relative to the scan root at all: a file: URI where a filesystem-absolute path belongs, beside a file_path naming a different file. Every value was derived by reading the fixture, the recorded runner metadata and the authored contracts in harness/lib/normalize/, and every anchor fact was checked against the pinned tree at 59b8a4489c878fa3a9aa6b7fbae760f2fc80eb9d -- never by running the adapter and recording what it printed. Where this file and harness/lib/normalize/adapters/checkov.py disagree, the disagreement is the finding: diagnose it rather than overwriting this file to match. It establishes two things at once: that AAP 0.8.2's no-absolute-path invariant is enforced on the way out of the resolver rather than assumed, and that a record whose two statements about its own location contradict each other is counted rather than resolved in favour of one. The class's other route on this tool -- a file_path with no anchor beside it -- is a separate document, reject-checkov-unresolvable-path, so that each fixture measures one attributable case.
scanner_class_note: Fixed for this tool by AAP 0.5.4's class table and carried unchanged on both rows. It does not vary with check_type, with the reporting framework or with record content; trivy is the single tool whose class is decided per record, from the section the record was read from. The rejected record carries no scanner_class at all, because it produces no row.

fixture.top_level_form_note: A single report object -- the form a Checkov artifact takes when one framework reports. The multi-framework array form is covered by oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/fixtures/checkov-alt-shape.json and is not re-covered here: this fixture's subject is path resolution, and testing one thing at a time is what makes a failure attributable.
fixture.summary_note: The report's own summary object, quoted as the fixture carries it. It is never used as the record count: the count unit below is the one normalize.reconcile.count_records walks independently of row construction. Here the two disagree, and the disagreement is deliberate -- see summary_disagreement_is_deliberate below. Agreement with the count unit is not the same as authority, and this is the document where that distinction is observable rather than merely asserted.
fixture.summary_disagreement_is_deliberate: The summary says failed 4 while results.failed_checks carries 3. The splice that built this fixture carried the envelope across untouched, which is the provenance-faithful choice for a whole-record derivation, and the mismatch it leaves is worth keeping: an adapter or a reconciler that read the summary instead of walking the array would report 4 where no traversal supports it, and this fixture would catch it. checkov-alt-shape.json carries the same property from the other direction -- its summary counts 201 passes while its results object has no passed array at all -- so the corpus already holds the tool's summary to be evidence about the tool rather than a substitute for the count.
fixture.derived_from: oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/fixtures/reject-checkov-unresolvable-path.json as first committed, at sha256 ce886a3db77d2eaa1287087a692135d77c58ae319751583cfcae35330cb625dc (11570 bytes, 4 failed checks), itself derived from oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/fixtures/derived-checkov-features.json, itself an excerpt of harness/artifacts/raw/checkov.json (sha256 d5e4492ac799875f6cf14c187f9130bc2ad3f8060c320e757c127dfd1fda98fc, 6 failed checks)
fixture.derivation: A negative fixture is derived from the captured one rather than being an excerpt of it, so the provenance is stated as a derivation. Two of the three failed checks are unmodified captured output: /results/failed_checks/0 is identical to the raw artifact's failed_checks[5] and to the positive fixture's failed_checks[4], and /results/failed_checks/2 is identical to the raw artifact's failed_checks[4] and the positive fixture's failed_checks[3]. The third, at /results/failed_checks/1, is the one synthesized defective record: a captured record whose file_abs_path was replaced with a file: URI naming a different real file and whose repo_file_path was nulled, with nothing else changed. It sits at index 1 rather than last so a kept row follows it, which is what makes the traversal-continues assertion mean something.
fixture.captured_provenance: Established by canonical-JSON comparison of every field of every record, not by eye. /results/failed_checks/1 agrees with the raw artifact's failed_checks[1] on 26 of its 28 fields, in the same key order, differing only in file_abs_path -- the captured absolute path replaced by a file: URI naming a different file -- and repo_file_path, nulled. So the sole defect is the record's statement about its own location: check_id, check_name, severity, file_line_range, check_result and every other field are the tool's own output. That isolation is the point: a fixture that changed a second field could not attribute the rejection to the path. The two kept records are the very elements the predecessor carried, byte for byte, and each is captured output at one further remove.
fixture.sibling_fixture_note: oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/fixtures/reject-checkov-unresolvable-path.json carries the same two captured records at the same two indexes and the class's other defective record at index 1. The two fixtures differ in exactly one element, which is what lets the pair be asserted against each other: identical rows, identical bucket counts, identical counters, and the rejection the only difference.
fixture.sha256_purpose: The recorded digest is what makes a later edit to the fixture visible. These expectations are re-derived when the fixture changes, never adjusted to keep a test green.

fixture_split.what_changed: This document and its fixture are the second half of a split. oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/fixtures/reject-checkov-unresolvable-path.json carried four failed checks and two rejections when it was first committed -- the two distinct routes this class has on this tool. This fixture carries the same two captured records and the second of those defective ones, so that each route is measured on its own.
fixture_split.why: AAP 0.9.4 asks a negative fixture to exercise a rejection condition, and a fixture assigned one attributable case may not quietly measure two: a suite that counted rejections would stay green while one of the two routes silently stopped being reached, and a reader looking for the case the fixture is named for would find two. The two records were not two instances of one route. They were the two distinct routes this class has on this tool, reached through different code in different modules, reporting record identities of different shapes -- so neither could stand in for the other.
fixture_split.how: A whole-record splice of the predecessor, taken from the committed document rather than re-serialized from a parsed copy: the failed_checks array was split into element blocks by brace depth, each block asserted to round-trip to exactly the element it came from, and three of the four reassembled -- the two captured records, and this route's defective one placed at index 1 -- with the other route's dropped. Every kept element's text appears verbatim in both the predecessor and this fixture, and the check_type member, all three other buckets, the summary object and both key orders are untouched.
fixture_split.where_the_other_route_lives: oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/fixtures/reject-checkov-unresolvable-path.json and oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/expected/reject-checkov-unresolvable-path.rows.json, which kept the original name and now carry the only_file_path route alone, with the same two kept records and their defective one at the same index.
fixture_split.coverage_is_not_reduced: Both routes are still exercised, one document each, and each document's rejection count is now the number its name promises. The pair also gained an invariant neither half had alone: the two fixtures differ in exactly one record, so their rows, their three bucket counts and all 28 of their counters must be identical and the rejection must be the only difference between them.
fixture_split.nothing_in_the_adapter_changed_for_this: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/checkov.py and harness/lib/normalize/paths.py were not edited. The split changes what the fixtures measure, not what the normalizer does, and both routes behave exactly as they did before.

routing.detected_by: normalize.shape -- this artifact is not SARIF and routes to the native adapter keyed by the runner that wrote it. It carries no version of "2.1.0" and no runs array, which together are the whole of the SARIF test.
routing.routing_decision: normalize.shape.route("checkov", doc) returns tool "checkov", shape "checkov", adapter "checkov", scanner_class "misconfig"
routing.not_a_shape_failure: No shape failure is expected here, and a test asserting one against this fixture would be asserting the wrong thing. The enclosing document is a well-formed Checkov report in its object form and routes cleanly; one record inside it is defective, and the adapter rejects that one while still emitting the others. The fixtures that own shape-detection failure are near-sarif-version-only.json, near-sarif-runs-only.json and unknown-shape.json.
routing.negative_routing_test: The mandated negative routing assertion -- that a native artifact must not route to the SARIF adapter -- belongs to test_shape_routing_negative.py. This fixture is eligible material for it, being native, but the assertion is that file's and is not restated here.

field_order_authority: harness/lib/normalize/emit.py, the FIELDS constant, of which harness/lib/normalize/adapters/checkov.py carries the authored copy AAP 0.6.4's import restriction requires. Every row below carries all twelve keys in that order, present-with-null rather than omitted.
absence_convention: Absence is JSON null here and in findings.json, and an empty field in findings.csv. tool, scanner_class, rule_id, message, severity_norm, path and in_scope are never absent -- exactly emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS -- so a record whose path cannot be resolved is rejected and counted rather than emitted with a null path.

allowlist.note: in_scope is decided by that file alone. The globs are not copied here: the allowlist is the single authority and stays byte-exact. The glob each row matched is recorded per row under row_derivations. That the runner also reads the allowlist to build its 18 -d target roots is a fact about its reach, not about this field.

resolution_context.worked_example: AAP 0.5.3's first user example, carried in unchanged. Checkov's file_path is relative to the scan target and carries a leading slash, alongside file_abs_path holding the filesystem-absolute path and repo_file_path a root-relative path that also carries a leading slash. The expected path is the leading slash stripped and the remainder treated as root-relative, reconciled against the absolute file_abs_path the same record carries. This fixture is the case where that reconciliation has something to catch.
resolution_context.path_base_source: harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json, the checkov entry's path_base -- read as input, never assumed
resolution_context.runner_invocation: one checkov invocation carrying 18 root-relative -d target roots, recorded at runner-metadata.json tools.checkov.invocation_form. This is the fact that makes file_path ambiguous on its own, and therefore the fact that makes an anchor field load-bearing rather than a convenience.
resolution_context.anchor_used: repo_file_path on both rows; the rejected record's only anchor cannot be expressed under any root
resolution_context.anchor_rule: repo_file_path is root-relative and carries a leading slash, so exactly one slash is stripped and the remainder is the row's path. file_abs_path is filesystem-absolute and is relativized to the scan root. The branch is chosen by which field it is, never by whether the value looks absolute -- which is the whole of the worked example, since repo_file_path looks filesystem-absolute while not being it.
resolution_context.file_path_role: corroboration only. Under per_target_directory the slash-stripped file_path is relative to whichever -d root matched, so it corroborates by being a suffix of the anchored path -- and it is, on both rows. A disagreement is recorded rather than resolved and never suppresses a row, and a file_path with no anchor beside it is not promoted to an anchor. Neither mechanism reaches the rejected record here: its anchor is present, so nothing is promoted, and the anchor is refused before a resolution exists for the disagreement to be recorded on.
resolution_context.why_file_path_alone_is_wrong: Stripping the slash off file_path and joining the remainder to the tree root names dockerfiles/spark/Dockerfile, a directory that does not exist at the root and which matches no allowlist glob, so every row would silently take in_scope false. Reading the same value as filesystem-absolute is the failure the worked example warns about: it relativizes to a long ../ chain, with nothing crashing. No expected path in this file begins with / or contains a ../ segment.
resolution_context.scan_root_source: harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json, spark_src and the checkov entry's resolved_scan_root
resolution_context.root_independence: Both rows below hold for whatever absolute scan root the adapter is given: each path comes from repo_file_path, which is already root-relative and needs no root to resolve. No row carries an absolute path in any field. The absolute values that do appear in this file are quoted evidence rather than emitted data -- the recorded scan root, each record's own anchor values under row_derivations and rejections, the parsing-error entry Checkov reported verbatim -- and none of them reaches a row. The rejection is root-independent for its own reason: a file: URI names nothing expressible under any root, so no choice of root could make it resolve.
resolution_context.severity_source: the record's own severity field, which is null on every failed check because severities require a licence and BC_API_KEY is deliberately absent. severity.resolve then states the absence rather than assuming a level: severity_native null, severity_norm Info, basis no_vocabulary. No CVSS score is consulted -- a misconfiguration carries none, and AAP 0.5.4's checkov row names severity and nothing else.
resolution_context.start_line_source: file_line_range[0], as an integer. The rejected record also carries a usable file_line_range of [1, 46], and it is never read: start_line is step 5 of the classification order and the path is step 4, so a record rejected on its path never reaches it.
resolution_context.cwe_and_cve_source: the closed field set guideline, description, short_description, bc_category, benchmarks, details, vulnerability_details. Every one of them is null or an empty array on every record here, so no CWE or CVE token exists to collect and both fields are null on both rows. check_name is deliberately outside that set: it is the row's message, and harvesting an identifier out of a message would put a weakness reference in the dataset that the record never made as a reference.
resolution_context.package_coordinate: null on both rows. A misconfiguration names a location in a configuration file rather than a package, so no coordinate can be formed -- and that absence is not a rejection: AAP 0.5.4 attaches unformable_package_coordinate to a dependency-oriented record, which this is not.

rejection_boundary.statement: A path that cannot be established is a rejection. A path that merely resolves somewhere unwanted is a kept row with in_scope false. The one defective record here resolves to nothing that may be emitted, which is what makes it the unresolvable_path case rather than one of the kept cases below.
rejection_boundary.why_it_can_only_be_a_rejection: path is one of only two never-absent fields in the twelve-field schema, the other being severity_norm: emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS carries path, and emit.OPTIONAL_FIELDS is exactly severity_native, start_line, cwe, cve and package_coordinate. A record with no resolvable path therefore has no valid row representation at all -- emit.validate_rows refuses a null path with the reason 'path and severity_norm are never absent: a record whose path could not be resolved was rejected and counted upstream' -- so counting it under a named class is the only outcome that neither drops the record nor invents a coordinate for it.
rejection_boundary.the_rejection_this_fixture_owns: /results/failed_checks/1 is the record this fixture is named for, and it fails for two independent reasons, both recorded because either alone would suffice. The anchor cannot be expressed against the scan root at all: paths.assert_relative_path refuses any value carrying a scheme in _EMITTED_PATH_FORBIDDEN_SCHEMES, and file is one of them, so no emitted path can be formed from it and ResolvedPath cannot even be constructed. And the record's two statements about its own location contradict each other -- file_path names a Dockerfile under dockerfiles/spark/bindings/python while file_abs_path names resource-managers/kubernetes/core/pom.xml, a different real file in a different directory -- with repo_file_path, which would ordinarily arbitrate, null. The two name different files, one a Dockerfile and one a Maven pom, and both really exist at the pin, so neither can be dismissed as obviously the corrupt one. AAP 0.1.3 forbids picking one: a record that cannot be attributed with certainty is rejected and the rejection recorded as a class with its count, never guessed into a field. Promoting file_path to fill the gap is unavailable too, because under per_target_directory it is relative to whichever of 18 -d roots matched and the scan root is not a substitute for that answer -- which is the sibling document's subject. The recorded detail speaks of the URI scheme because the resolver reaches the unexpressible-anchor guard before the disagreement can be attached to anything: the disagreement is the substantive fault and the scheme is the mechanism by which it surfaces. A fixture whose anchor merely disagreed while remaining expressible would produce a kept row with the disagreement recorded, which is a different behaviour with its own coverage note below.
rejection_boundary.the_sibling_route: The class's other route is not restated here as a hazard, because it is not absent by accident: it has its own fixture and its own expected file, oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/expected/reject-checkov-unresolvable-path.rows.json, carrying a record whose only path field is a target-relative file_path. path_resolution_routes above is the authoritative map of the two, and this document is deliberately silent on the other's behaviour beyond naming where it lives.
rejection_boundary.pairing_with_the_positive_fixture: The pairing is the point of the pair. oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/expected/derived-checkov-features.rows.json proves the leading slash is honoured: five records whose consistent triples all resolve, with path_corroboration_recorded 0. This file proves the file_abs_path reconciliation is a real check rather than decoration -- and it is reliable precisely because the runner passes one -d per expanded absolute directory, which is what makes file_path target-relative and an anchor field the only thing that can place a record in the tree. Read together, the two files establish that the adapter honours the convention and still refuses a record the convention cannot place. Either file alone would leave the other half unproven.

mechanisms_not_used.mechanism: a leading slash on file_path treated as the fault
mechanisms_not_used.why_not: A leading slash on file_path is correct Checkov convention -- it is the user's own worked example -- and treating it as a defect would encode a bug into this suite and contradict the example it exists to carry. Every record in this fixture, the two rows included, carries a leading slash on file_path, and none is rejected for it.

AAP 0.8.3 makes those kept rows with in_scope false, counted under rows_out_of_scope. Out of scope means kept and marked, never rejected: only evidence about the runner establishes a wrong scan root, and an individual coordinate outside the twelve globs is a legitimate coordinate. Rejecting one here would assert the opposite of what the AAP requires.

rejection_boundary.fault_verified_from_the_fixture: Checked rather than assumed, in both directions. The defective record differs from its captured original -- the raw artifact's failed_checks[1] -- in exactly its two anchor fields and in nothing else: 26 of 28 fields identical by canonical comparison, in the same key order, so the fault cannot be anything but the path. And it trips no earlier classification step: it is a JSON object, it carries a non-empty check_id, and it carries a non-empty check_name, so steps 1 to 3 all pass and the path is the only thing left to reject it for.

not_a_rejection.case: a path resolving outside the twelve authoritative globs
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false, counted under rows_out_of_scope
not_a_rejection.evidence: This runner legitimately reaches such coordinates, since its reach is shaped by its 18 -d roots while in_scope is the allowlist's answer and not the runner's.

not_a_rejection.case: an anchor disagreement that is nonetheless expressible
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row on the first anchor in the recorded order, with the disagreement recorded in the resolution's corroboration and counted under path_corroboration_recorded
not_a_rejection.evidence: paths.resolve_checkov_path reconciles the anchors against each other and records a mismatch rather than resolving it, and the corroboration never suppresses a row. This fixture's defective record does carry a disagreement between its file_path and its anchor, but that anchor is a file: URI, so the record is refused before any row exists to record the note on -- which is why path_corroboration_recorded is 0 below and not 1. The behaviour itself, a kept row carrying a recorded disagreement, is covered by neither this document nor its sibling and is listed under behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture below.

not_a_rejection.case: a path in a src/test tree
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false
not_a_rejection.evidence: The exclusion is literal -- a path containing src/test is out of scope -- and it removes the path from scope rather than from the dataset.

not_a_rejection.case: a passed check, a skipped check or a parsing error
not_a_rejection.evidence: See failures_only below. A parsing error in particular is Checkov's own report about a file it could not read, not a finding this adapter could not attribute; converting one into a rejection would put it on the right-hand side of the identity while the independent traversal never put it on the left.

rejection_boundary.no_guessed_path: The rejected record is not given a path. Nothing in this file supplies a coordinate for it, not even a plausible one -- and here the plausible candidates, the two locations the record itself names, are exactly what is being refused.

path_resolution_routes.authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py resolve_checkov_path, and the narrow paths.PathPolicyError catch in harness/lib/normalize/adapters/checkov.py _adapt_failed_check. Read from the two modules rather than from a summary of them, because the routes differ in which module builds the rejection.

routes.reached_by: no anchor field yields a usable value, a slash-stripped file_path corroborator is present, and the recorded path_base.kind is per_target_directory rather than scan_root -- resolve_checkov_path's final branch, returned to the adapter and passed through as-is.
routes.identity_built_by: paths.resolve_checkov_path, from check_id, file_path and repo_file_path with any of the three that is null omitted
routes.detail_opens_with: the failed check carries only file_path (

routes.reached_by: an anchor field is present and yields a value, but constructing the ResolvedPath from it runs paths.assert_relative_path, which raises paths.PathPolicyError -- for a leading slash, a backslash or UNC prefix, a Windows drive prefix, a URI authority, a forbidden URI scheme, more than one archive separator, or anything PurePosixPath or PureWindowsPath calls absolute. The adapter catches it and converts it, re-raising RunnerMetadataError first because that subclass is a caller fault rather than a defective record.
routes.identity_built_by: the adapter, from report_index, check_index, check_type and check_id
routes.detail_opens_with: the failed check's path fields cannot be expressed against the scan root:

path_resolution_routes.why_this_route_is_the_dangerous_one: Recorded because the two routes fail differently, not merely differently-shaped. The sibling route's failure mode is a plausible-looking wrong answer: a resolver that promoted the bare file_path would emit dockerfiles/spark/bindings/R/Dockerfile, a legal relative path that names nothing and silently takes in_scope false. This route's failure mode is a value no consumer could read as a path at all -- a scheme-bearing absolute URI in the dataset's path column, which AAP 0.8.2 forbids outright. assert_relative_path is the guard, it runs on every ResolvedPath construction so no resolver can bypass it, and this is the document that proves it fires on real record content rather than only on hand-made input.
path_resolution_routes.the_two_identities_differ_in_shape: Authored rather than accidental, and a test must expect it. paths.py names the class and writes the sub-reason for the route it decides itself, and the adapter returns that Rejection unreworded, so the identity is the record's own fields. Where the adapter catches an exception instead, paths.py never got as far as building a Rejection, so the adapter supplies the identity from the coordinates it holds. Rewording either one to match the other would lose the information about which module refused the record.
path_resolution_routes.why_two_documents: Each route fails a different implementation. A resolver that promoted a bare file_path to an anchor would pass the unexpressible-anchor document and fail this one; a resolver that emitted an anchor value without running it through assert_relative_path would pass this one and fail that. One fixture carrying both would be green while either half regressed.
path_resolution_routes.no_third_route: resolve_checkov_path's other two return values are different classes -- absent_path where the record names no location at all, and malformed_record where the record is not an object, which the adapter's step 1 reaches first -- so unresolvable_path has exactly these two routes on this tool. reject-checkov-absent-path and reject-checkov-malformed-record own those.

failures_only.count_unit: one element of results.failed_checks[], the union across every report object in either top-level shape
failures_only.passed_checks_note: Neither counted nor emitted, and neither check_id may appear anywhere in the rows array. Both pass on resource-managers/kubernetes/docker/src/main/dockerfiles/spark/Dockerfile because line 71 of that file is USER ${spark_uid} -- the last instruction, and not root. CKV_DOCKER_3 in particular is the check the same file's CKV_DOCKER_2 failure sits beside, so a bucket-blind adapter would emit a row for a check that genuinely passed. They are observable only through the passed_checks_observed counter, which is what makes produced-no-row an observation rather than a claim.
failures_only.skipped_checks_note: Neither counted nor emitted, exactly as passed checks are not. The one entry is CKV_DOCKER_9 on bindings/R/Dockerfile at file_line_range [34, 37] carrying a suppress_comment, and it must produce no row even though the identical check_id on the main Dockerfile does -- the bucket decides that, never the check_id. It names a file no failed check in this fixture names, which is the one respect in which this document is milder than its sibling: there the skipped entry sits on the same file as the rejected failed check and must not be read as supplying the anchor that record is missing. Here the rejected record's anchor is present and unexpressible, so there is nothing a neighbour could be mistaken for supplying.
failures_only.parsing_errors_note: Status evidence for oss-scan-results/tool-status.md, carried verbatim, and neither a finding nor a rejection. The distinction matters more in this fixture than in the positive one, because this document does contain a rejection: a reader could reasonably expect the parsing error to join it. It must not. A rejection describes a failed check this adapter could not attribute; a parsing error is the tool's report about a file it never turned into a check, and it is not one of the counted failed checks. Counting it would make rejections 2 while the independent traversal still returned 3, breaking the identity for something that was never a finding. The named file exists at the pin: it is a shell script the dockerfile framework does not parse.
failures_only.vacuity_note: The three zero expectations above are why this fixture carries non-empty passed_checks, skipped_checks and parsing_errors at all. Against an artifact whose buckets were empty -- which is what the raw artifact's --compact output is -- the failures-only contract would be satisfied by an adapter that read every bucket, and the assertion would prove nothing.

counts.raw_count_unit: one element of results.failed_checks[] -- the unit normalize.reconcile.count_records walks independently of row construction
counts.raw_count_authority: normalize.reconcile.count_records("checkov", doc), whose traversal reduces both top-level shapes to a sequence of report objects and sums the length of each results.failed_checks array, building no row, resolving no path and mapping no severity. It reads reconcile.CHECKOV_COUNTED_SECTION and nothing else, so passed_checks, skipped_checks and parsing_errors contribute zero by construction. It is the independent half of the identity: a count taken from the traversal that builds the rows would satisfy the assertion while testing nothing.
counts.rejection_class_count_note: One class, one record under it -- the number this fixture's name promises. The class covers two routes on this tool and each now owns a document: this one is the unexpressible-anchor route, and the only_file_path route is oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/expected/reject-checkov-unresolvable-path.rows.json. Recording the route in the rejection's detail while the class carries the count is what AAP 0.5.4 asks of a class that covers several routes; splitting the two into separate fixtures is what keeps each count attributable.
counts.reconciliation_status_authority: normalize.reconcile, STATUS_PASS = "pass". Its STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE and the verdict reconcile.NOT_APPLICABLE_ABSENT are for a tool that wrote no artifact and are not in play here: this artifact exists and carries records.

four_reported_counters.authority: AAP 0.5.4 -- the four counts reported per tool
four_reported_counters.note: Named here rather than restated with their values. The counters block below is the single measurement, and a number carried twice inside one document is a number that can drift; counters_note gives the reason each of the four is zero.

counts.parse_status_authority: harness/lib/normalize/cli.py, PARSE_STATUS_PARTIAL = "partial", assigned as partial where there are rejections and clean where there are none. Partial is right precisely because the adapter did not abandon the artifact: every parsable record was emitted and both rejected records are counted under their class, with their reasons retained. This is deliberately not normalize.reconcile's STATUS_PASS / STATUS_FAIL / STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE vocabulary, which describes an assertion's outcome rather than an artifact's parse -- and note that the two co-exist here: the parse is partial while the reconciliation assertion passes.
counts.row_count_note: 2 is not len(results.failed_checks): it is that length minus the one rejected record. Two passed checks, one skipped check and one parsing error sit in the same document, and any one of them leaking in would make this 3, 4, 5 or 6, while a rejected record silently coerced into a row would make it 3 with the identity still balancing -- which is why the rejections array below is asserted by class and detail rather than by count alone. The tool's own summary says failed 4, and reading that instead of the array would make it 4.

counters_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/checkov.py, COUNTER_KEYS as returned by new_counters(): nineteen authored keys, one path_kind_* per member of normalize.paths.PATH_KINDS and one severity_basis_* per member of normalize.severity.BASIS_VALUES -- twenty-eight in all, every one an int.
counters_note: Four values a reader must not 'correct'. First, path_corroboration_recorded is 0, not 1, even though /results/failed_checks/1 does carry a file_path that disagrees with its anchor: the counter is incremented from a resolution that came back, and that record's resolution never came back, because constructing it raised on the anchor's URI scheme. The disagreement is reported in the rejection's detail instead, which is where a record with no row has to report anything. Second, every severity and path_kind counter is 2 rather than 3: severity is step 6 of the record walk and the path is step 4, so the rejected record never reaches a severity or contributes a path kind, and there is deliberately no adapter-side count of records walked, rows or rejections -- those are returned to the caller directly, and the independent left-hand side of the identity is normalize.reconcile.count_records. Third, start_line_absent is 0 because both rows carry a usable file_line_range; the rejected record also carries one and is never asked for it. Fourth, the four counters AAP 0.5.4 has reported per tool are all 0: caller_file_path is null on every record so none names a second location, no record carries a CWE or CVE identifier in the closed source field set, and both emitted paths name a file inside the scanned tree.
counters_root_note: Given some other absolute scan root, no counter above changes and no row changes. Both rows take their path from repo_file_path, which needs no root; the rejection is root-independent because a file: URI is unexpressible under any root. The positive sibling's path_corroboration_recorded is root-dependent because its records carry two resolvable anchors that would disagree under a different root; here the only record with a second anchor is rejected before any note can be recorded, so even that dependency is absent.

rejections.locator_note: The pointer and the report_index / check_index pair name the same record, and here the pair is also the identity: normalize.adapters.checkov catches the paths.PathPolicyError and passes exactly report_index, check_index, check_type and check_id into the rejection it builds, because paths.py never got as far as building one. The sibling document's rejection carries a different identity shape for that reason -- there paths.py decided the class itself and supplied the record's own fields. The asymmetry is authored rather than accidental and a test must expect it; path_resolution_routes above records why.
rejections.reject_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_UNRESOLVABLE_PATH constant -- a literal member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES, the closed set of ten. Written verbatim rather than paraphrased, and asserted against the module rather than by eye: a test that only counts rejections cannot tell one condition from another, so the class name is what carries the assertion.
rejections.classification_step: step 4 of the adapter's fixed classification order -- shape, rule identifier, message, path, start_line. Steps 1 to 3 all pass on this record: it is a JSON object, it carries check_id CKV_DOCKER_2, and it carries a non-empty check_name. That is deliberate, so the only thing left to reject it for is its path.
rejections.start_line_never_examined: Step 5 is never reached, so this record's file_line_range of [1, 46] is never examined and non_integer_start_line is not in play. Worth stating because the fixture does give the defective record a usable range, and a reader could otherwise expect an interaction between the two conditions.
rejections.produced_by: paths.PathPolicyError raised inside paths.resolve_checkov_path and caught by the adapter, which converts it to a counted rejection rather than letting it discard the whole artifact. RunnerMetadataError is caught first and re-raised, being a subclass -- a metadata fault is a caller fault, not a defective record.
rejections.normalisation_note: paths.normalise_reported_path drops empty interior segments, so the URI's // authority separator collapses and the value reaches assert_relative_path as a scheme-bearing reference rather than as a // authority. Either shape is refused; this is the one that actually occurs, and the recorded detail quotes it.
rejections.why_unresolvable: Two independent reasons, both true of this record. The anchor cannot be expressed against the scan root at all: paths.assert_relative_path refuses a value carrying a URI scheme in _EMITTED_PATH_FORBIDDEN_SCHEMES, and file is one of them, so no emitted path can be formed from it and ResolvedPath cannot even be constructed. And the record's two statements about its location contradict each other -- file_path names a Dockerfile under dockerfiles/spark/bindings/python while file_abs_path names resource-managers/kubernetes/core/pom.xml, a different real file in a different directory -- with repo_file_path null, so nothing arbitrates. file_path cannot be promoted to fill the gap either, because under per_target_directory it is relative to whichever of 18 -d roots matched and the scan root is not a substitute for that answer.
rejections.expected_detail: the failed check's path fields cannot be expressed against the scan root: 'file:/opt/spark-src/resource-managers/kubernetes/core/pom.xml' carries the URI scheme 'file', not a path relative to the root
rejections.expected_detail_note: The detail is the sub-reason AAP 0.5.4 requires a rejection to carry, and it is quoted here because this class covers two routes: naming the class alone would not distinguish this record from the sibling document's, which is the same class for a different reason. A test may assert the class exactly and the detail by its distinguishing substrings rather than by full-string equality, since the detail is prose that quotes the record's own value.
distinguishing_substrings: cannot be expressed against the scan root
expected_detail_must_not_contain: the scan root is not a substitute for the answer
rejections.distinguishing_substrings_note: The class is shared with the sibling document and sits one field away from absent_path, so the detail is what separates them. The forbidden list is the other two routes' own wording: the first two phrases belong to the only_file_path route and the third to absent_path, and either appearing here would mean the record was refused for a reason this fixture did not arrange.
rejections.sole_rejection: The only rejection this fixture produces. rejections is 1 and rejections_by_class is {unresolvable_path: 1}, and a second entry of any class would mean the fixture had acquired a defect it was not built to carry.
rejections.record_identity_note: These four keys are the adapter's own, supplied at the point it catches the error, which is why this identity differs in shape from the next rejection's. Enough to find the record in the artifact again, and never the record itself and never a secret value.
rejections.why_not_a_row: There is no path to put in the row. path is never absent from a row, so a record whose coordinate cannot be expressed has no valid row representation, and the alternatives -- dropping it, or giving it one of its two contradictory candidates -- would each hide it. Counting it under a named class keeps it visible and keeps the arithmetic honest.
rejections.why_not_a_recorded_corroboration: A disagreement between a record's path fields is ordinarily recorded on the row and counted under path_corroboration_recorded, never rejected. That route needs a row to record the note on, and this record cannot produce one, because the anchor the note would qualify is itself unexpressible. So the disagreement is reported in the detail instead, and path_corroboration_recorded stays 0.
rejections.why_not_invalid_uri: invalid_uri is for an entry whose URI is syntactically invalid. This one is syntactically valid: it parses cleanly as a file: URI and names a file that exists at the pin. What disqualifies it is that a valid URI is not a path relative to the root, which is the unresolvable_path case.
rejections.why_not_absent_path: absent_path is for a record that carries no path field or an empty one. This record carries two, and they disagree.
rejections.contributes_no_severity_literal: The rejected record is never fed to the severity tally, so no native literal from it reaches severity-map.md. That document reports literals against the rows the dataset contains, and this record contributes none. Its severity is null in any case, which is exactly what makes the omission easy to miss and worth stating.

scope_of_this_file.records_only_this_tool: These are checkov's rows and rejections and nothing else. Trivy also reports misconfigurations on the same Dockerfile, and that produces trivy's own rows in trivy's own expected file: no comparison, no deduplication, no ranking and no cross-tool interpretation is made here, and nothing in this file characterises a finding as real, important or a false positive. Two tools reporting the same location produce two rows and no comment.
scope_of_this_file.no_secret_value: No field carries a secret or any content from check_result.results_configuration. message is check_name and nothing else, so the multi-line shell text those records quote -- including the apt invocations and the pam.d redirection -- reaches no row and no rejection detail. The absolute paths that appear are quoted evidence about the fixture, never emitted data. This tree is committed to git.
scope_of_this_file.no_inference: A record whose path could not be established with certainty is a counted rejection, never one of the two candidates the record itself offers. This file is where that rule is exercised for checkov's unexpressible-anchor route, and the rule is why the fixture yields two rows and one rejection rather than three rows.
scope_of_this_file.no_judgement_of_the_findings: That the anchor Dockerfile has no HEALTHCHECK is recorded as the reason CKV_DOCKER_2 fires and therefore as evidence the row is real tool output. It is not a claim that the finding matters, and no remediation is suggested anywhere.
